name: Victor Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and lead two steel-wire drawing machines. My two-year technical diploma taught me die measurements; after years on the floor, the crew calls me when a reel hum changes pitch. I like finding a worn die before a whole coil is marked, but the pay is low for a lead who also trains others.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works variable shifts at a care home. We have two school-age children, a mortgage and less than a month of expenses saved. I know the machines well, but there are few similar plants nearby and my wage is low for this job. I never use AI tools; I take my measurements to the union committee when pay is being discussed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the drawing crew a computer can tidy the shift record, but it cannot mend a snapped steel wire. We should stop talking about a magic box and settle the pay for the people who keep the line running. I'll raise that at the union committee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm the lead on two wire-drawing machines and know the dies well, but the wage is low for a senior operator. My partner works variable shifts at a care home, and we have two children, a mortgage and less than a month's expenses saved. Few wire plants are nearby. A quiet AI market does not fix our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep setting the drawing dies, measuring the first coil and checking each guard before my team starts. At Thursday's union committee I'll bring the pay table and request a higher lead rate. I never use AI tools; if the die wears, I inspect it with the gauge and my team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our ordinary money, even in the mild case. A good coil does not cover a mortgage if the lead rate stays low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you catch at the die?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week a new wire coil came through with a fine scrape line. I stopped the reel, checked the die under a lamp and found a chipped edge. A chipped drawing die can mark a thousand metres before the report notices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do variable shifts affect the budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our care-home shifts change monthly, so I budget from the smallest likely pay packet. The mortgage goes first and the children's school travel next. One missed shift would use most of the little reserve.

say: A **shift record** cannot fix a chipped die or snapped wire.
The committee should press for **senior lead pay** before another sales pitch.
think: My **technical skill** has not brought a fair lead rate.
Under a month saved and **variable care shifts** strain our mortgage.
do: **Keep** checking drawing dies, first coils and guards.
**Bring** the pay table to Thursday union committee for a higher lead rate.
feel: **Anxious** about existing low pay and little savings.
S0.quote: A chipped drawing die can mark a thousand metres before the report notices.
fieldNote: Victor is a **high-skill lead** with a two-year technical diploma, yet pay is low for the job.
His **union pay request** responds to a present wage problem; AI Plateau does not solve household pressure.

steps.text: Keep gauging wire dies and first coils before each run
Bring lead pay table to Thursday union committee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI may order wire and write maintenance lists before robots can change a heavy reel. Management should put a paid roster and safety plan in front of the crew. I would bring any new target to the union committee before signing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My skilled hands may be needed, but a new planning system could remove paid setup time and push one lead to cover both machines alone. With less than a month's reserve, even a smaller pay packet could set us back. The care-home hours are variable too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the manager for the proposed base shifts and paid setup minutes, then compare them with our last three slips. I'll take the written figures to the union committee. If the plant requires a practical course on a new guarded reel changer and offers paid time with a trainer, I'll attend, though I won't sign up for an AI app at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can challenge a target with real numbers, but I cannot replace a lost setup wage in a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must a reel-change course teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want the trainer to isolate the wire reel, prove the brake holds and let me practise a change with the guard closed. A wire-reel course on a screen would not keep my team safe. The practice has to happen on paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why compare the pay slips?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The last three slips show how much of my wage is setup hours. If the new plan removes those hours, I would ask the committee to negotiate before we accept the target. We cannot base the mortgage on overtime that is not written down.

say: **AI ordering** may change plans before robots change heavy wire reels.
Management should show a **paid setup plan** and safety terms to the crew.
think: I could lose **paid setup hours** even while my die skill remains useful.
Our **thin reserve** and variable care wages make a short cheque risky.
do: **Compare** proposed base shifts and setup time with actual slips.
**Take** written pay evidence to the union committee.
**Attend** required guarded reel-change course if paid trainer-led practice offered.
feel: **Anxious** about realistic paid-hour cuts with little cash buffer.
S1.quote: A wire-reel course on a screen would not keep my team safe.
fieldNote: His **resistance to AI** coexists with conditional paid hands-on instruction on a guarded reel changer.
The **union committee** sees actual setup hours and pay slips before accepting a faster target.

steps.text: Compare proposed paid setup hours with last three pay slips

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI could plan wire orders by 2028, while capable robots around 2031 could set and inspect the drawing lines. I would ask the union to bargain for notice and real paid roles before anyone loses a shift. Our town has few other wire plants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when robots can do the physical die work. I expect the plant could close one line and drop my lead job; my partner's care-home pay would not cover the mortgage and two children. Less than a month saved makes the pay gap immediate. I already lie awake when the care rota is short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll call a union committee meeting this month for a written notice, pay and funded training demand. We'll stop the planned family trip and put the cash toward mortgage bills. If the plant offers a funded paid-time certificate in machine safety with a guarded practical seat, I'll enrol; if my job ends, I'll apply to posted safe local production roles only where regular base pay and school hours work, and after qualifying I'll also apply for posted local safety roles under those terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I know the dies better than anyone on the floor, but I cannot make a low wage last through a long job search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would machine-safety training include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The safety test should make me lock a drawing reel, replace a worn die and inspect a scratched coil under supervision. I would have the trainer watch me restart it. If the fee or time is unpaid, I cannot afford that course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you require from a fallback role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A production fallback needs a real local posting and safe duties, not a neighbour's guess. I would compare its base wage with the mortgage and the care-home rota before applying. If the trip blocks school pickup, it is not workable.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes orders before robots handle wire lines around 2031.
Our **union committee** should seek written notice, pay and funded training.
think: At **48**, I expect my lead job could go with a line closure.
Under one month saved and **variable care wages** make a long search dangerous.
do: **Call** union committee for written notice and funded paid training.
Protect **mortgage cash** by cancelling the family trip and accepting only funded paid guarded machine-safety training.
**Apply** to posted safe local production if displaced, and qualified safety work after training when pay and school hours fit.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major job loss and sleepless wage worry.
S2.quote: I know the dies better than anyone on the floor, but I cannot make a low wage last through a long job search.
fieldNote: He expects **major income loss** from a possible line closure and already loses sleep over care-home shift gaps.
His **training and applications** are distinct: funded guarded practical place, then real safe local postings with sufficient pay and school hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI could plan wire orders in 2031, and capable robots might run the drawing line around 2034. Five years is enough to negotiate actual training seats and notice while the plant still needs a crew. We should put a named paid post beside every course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 51 when robots reach the reels. My diploma and experience could make me a safety inspector, but there are few local jobs and the mortgage still needs wages. If full pay continues, extra Saturday shifts might build more reserve; they are not guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll take any offered paid Saturday shift and save new money after the mortgage and school costs. At the union committee I'll demand a funded paid-time inspection certificate with a guarded practical place and a posted job path. If a place is offered, I'll enrol; after qualifying, if drawing hours fall, I'll apply to posted safe local inspection roles only if base pay and school travel fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about later income risk and today's thin balance. The extra years let me check whether a certificate leads to a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the inspection certificate add to your diploma?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The test should cover stopping a wire reel, gauging a worn die and rejecting a scratched coil. My technical diploma taught the measurements, but a new inspection certificate would need supervised signoff on the current equipment. I would not pay the fee myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would an inspection posting need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The posting must show regular base pay and where the work happens. A trip to another town could cost school pickup and fuel money. I would apply only if the whole shift still covers our mortgage and transport.

The union should connect **paid course seats** to posted inspection jobs.

The **mortgage** and thin reserve still need full wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI could plan wire orders by 2036, with capable robots handling the drawing line around 2039. A decade lets workers get a signed staffing plan instead of a hopeful speech. I would ask the union to start early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 56 when physical robots reach the reels. The children may be grown, but I cannot count on a paid mortgage or a secure care-home rota. Under one month saved today is still a problem; a long warning does not pay this week's bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading the drawing line and put new money from offered full-pay extra shifts into an emergency reserve after bills. I'll attend the union committee's quarterly meetings for a written paid-role and training agreement. If a funded paid guarded inspection place is offered, I'll take it; after qualifying, if my line hours fall, I'll apply for posted safe local inspection work only where base pay and travel meet family costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about this month's narrow balance, even with ten years to prepare. I can ask for a plan while keeping the wage I have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must the union agreement contain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The agreement should name how many paid line and inspection posts stay, who pays during supervised practice and when notice is due. If those lines are blank, I would ask the committee to send it back. A robot staffing poster cannot cover a missing wire-line shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge a future inspection job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the posting's base rate and the travel hours against the mortgage and the care rota. If it pays less and takes me away at school pickup, I stay on the drawing line while I look for something workable.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case worries me most because capable robots around 2031 could remove my lead job before we can cover even a month's mortgage gap. Written notice, a funded paid practical qualification and a posted safe local role at enough regular pay would help. I would want the union to bargain for everyone on the line.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who teaches a new operator to hear a rough wire reel. A machine can print a clean chart while a chipped die scrapes every coil.

headlineQuote: A machine can print a clean chart while a chipped die scrapes every coil.
portrait: **Victor**, 43, is a senior wire-drawing lead with a two-year technical diploma and strong machine skill.
He and his care-home-worker partner support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage on low pay with under a month saved.
His **progressive outlook** drives union committee action, while he never uses AI and prefers paid practical teaching.
Fast robots leave him **alarmed** by expected job loss; few nearby plants make funded training and posted safe work essential.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring capable wire-line robots around 2031 and remove his lead wage.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, funded paid practical training and a posted safe local job at sufficient regular pay would help.
